slides.title: Three transformer flavors
slides.body:
Not every transformer is shaped the same way. Three variants dominate:

- **Encoder-only**: BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa. Bidirectional attention; trained with masked language modeling. Good for embedding, classification, retrieval. Not used for free-form generation.
- **Decoder-only**: GPT-2/3/4, LLaMA, Mistral, Claude (architecturally). Causal masking; trained with next-token prediction. Generates text autoregressively. This is the dominant LLM shape today.
- **Encoder-decoder**: T5, BART, the original transformer paper. An encoder reads the input bidirectionally; a decoder generates the output autoregressively, attending back to the encoder's output via cross-attention. Used for translation, summarization, structured tasks.

The decision tree: do you need to generate text? Decoder-only or encoder-decoder. Do you have a clear input/output split (translation, summarization)? Encoder-decoder might help. Are you embedding or classifying? Encoder-only.

The heatmap shows a **dense, unmasked self-attention matrix** — the kind used inside an encoder. Every token attends to every other token, including future positions. Compare this to the strictly lower-triangular pattern of a decoder's causal mask: the encoder has no forbidden positions, giving it a bidirectional view of the whole sequence.

slides.title: Encoder-only
slides.body:
An encoder is N transformer blocks where attention is **bidirectional** — every token attends to every other token, with no masking.

```
input tokens: [token_1, token_2, ..., token_N]
  ↓ embed + position
  ↓ encoder blocks (N x)
output: per-token contextualized representations [h_1, h_2, ..., h_N]
```

BERT-style training masks out 15% of tokens randomly and asks the model to predict them. This forces every position to learn from both left and right context, producing rich representations.

Use cases:
- **Embeddings** (sentence, paragraph, or document) for retrieval / clustering
- **Classification** — pass the [CLS] token's hidden state through a linear layer
- **Token-level tasks** — NER, parsing, QA span prediction

Encoders can't generate text in any natural way. To generate, you need autoregression.

slides.title: Decoder-only — the modern LLM
slides.body:
A decoder is N transformer blocks where attention is **causal**: token at position `t` can only attend to positions `1..t`. This is the [[masked-self-attention]] pattern — the upper triangle of the attention matrix is masked to `-inf` before softmax.

Why causal? It enables **autoregressive generation**: predict token `t+1` from `1..t`, then concatenate and repeat. The same forward pass during training computes all next-token predictions in parallel (one per position), so training is efficient.

GPT-2/3/4, Claude, Gemini, LLaMA — all decoder-only. The reason: a single decoder-only model trained on lots of text can do classification, generation, retrieval-via-prompting, and so on, all from the same weights. Encoder-only and encoder-decoder are less flexible at the same scale.

The modern shape:
```
decoder block (causal attention) × N
final LN
unembed → vocab logits
```

question.question: Why can't a BERT-style encoder-only model generate text autoregressively?
options: Its attention is bidirectional — every position sees both past and future tokens, so there's no clean way to generate one token at a time
It uses the wrong activation function
Encoders don't have an unembedding layer
question.explanation: Generation requires causal masking: token t depends only on tokens 1..t-1. With bidirectional attention, the encoder uses the *entire* input including future positions. There's no way to call a bidirectional model on a partial input and trust the output, because at training every position saw the full context.

slides.title: Encoder-decoder
slides.body:
Encoder-decoder transformers have two stacks:

1. **Encoder** processes the input bidirectionally — same as BERT.
2. **Decoder** generates the output autoregressively, but in addition to causal self-attention, each layer also does **cross-attention** to the encoder's output.

```
encoder(input) → encoder_states
decoder block:
  causal self-attention(decoder_states)
  cross-attention(decoder_Q, encoder_states_K, encoder_states_V)
  FFN
```

Cross-attention lets the decoder pull information from the input as it generates. This is intuitive for translation: as you generate French token by token, you keep referring back to the English source.

T5 and BART are the canonical encoder-decoder models. They're still excellent for tasks with a clean input/output split, but for general-purpose chat / completion, decoder-only models have largely won — partly because of scale, partly because cross-attention adds parameters that don't help open-ended generation as much as bigger decoders do.

question.question: What does cross-attention do in an encoder-decoder model?
options: Lets each decoder layer attend back to the encoder's output, so the decoder can reference the input as it generates
Mixes encoder and decoder weights together
question.explanation: Cross-attention is in addition to self-attention, not a replacement. In each decoder layer: self-attention over previously-generated tokens, then cross-attention with Q from decoder state and K/V from encoder output. This is how the decoder 'sees' the input it's translating/summarizing.

question.question: Derive the encoder-decoder information flow and explain the role of bidirectionality vs causality
question.goal: Trace how the original Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) splits work between encoder and decoder: the encoder produces a rich bidirectional representation; the decoder uses it autoregressively via cross-attention.

steps.prompt: The encoder runs self-attention with NO causal mask. What does this mean for each token's representation at the output?
steps.motivation: Understanding full bidirectionality motivates why encoders produce richer per-token context than decoders.

acceptedAnswers: each token can attend to all other tokens, including future tokens
every token attends to all positions in both directions

hints: No masking means the attention matrix has no forbidden positions.
steps.reveal: Without a mask, every token attends to every other token — past and future. By the final encoder layer, each token's hidden state is a contextualized summary of the entire input sequence, not just what came before it. This is why encoder representations (as in BERT) are richer for understanding tasks than decoder representations.

steps.prompt: The decoder generates tokens one at a time at inference. Which attention mechanism prevents it from seeing future output tokens during training?
steps.motivation: Connecting causal masking to the decoder's autoregressive objective.
hints: The upper triangle of the decoder's self-attention score matrix is set to -∞ before softmax.
steps.reveal: The decoder uses causal (masked) self-attention: score matrix entries S[i,j] are set to -∞ for j > i before softmax, preventing position i from attending to any future output position. This makes training equivalent to N parallel autoregressive predictions over the target sequence.

steps.prompt: The decoder also has a cross-attention sublayer. What are Q, K, V in that sublayer, and what computation does it enable?
steps.motivation: Cross-attention is the bridge between the two stacks — naming it precisely closes the derivation.

acceptedAnswers: Q from decoder, K and V from encoder output
Q = decoder state, K = encoder output, V = encoder output

hints: The decoder is generating (provides queries); the encoder has the source context (provides keys and values).
steps.reveal: Cross-attention: Q = decoder hidden state (current generation step), K = encoder output, V = encoder output. Each decoder step can attend to any encoder position with full bidirectional context. This is how the decoder 'reads' the source input at every generation step — the key mechanism Vaswani et al. (2017) introduced in 'Attention Is All You Need' (NeurIPS 2017).

question.finalResult: Encoder (bidirectional self-attention, no mask) → full-context representations. Decoder (causal self-attention + cross-attention to encoder) → autoregressive generation conditioned on the full source. The split is: encoder understands, decoder generates while attending back to that understanding.

question.question: Choosing between encoder-decoder and decoder-only for a new task
question.prompt: Your team is building a system that takes a 500-word legal document as input and must produce a structured 3-sentence summary in a fixed format. A colleague argues for a decoder-only model (like LLaMA) with the document prepended as context; you argue for an encoder-decoder model (like T5 or BART). Make the case for encoder-decoder: explain (1) why bidirectional encoding of the source document is beneficial here, (2) how cross-attention allows each summary token to reference any part of the 500-word source, and (3) one scenario where the decoder-only approach would actually be preferable despite these advantages.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
The architecture-flavor decision is largely settled today: decoder-only for general-purpose LLMs, encoder-only for embeddings, encoder-decoder for specific input→output tasks where the bifurcation helps.

With all three shapes covered, the next conceptual piece is [[masked-self-attention]] — how the causal mask actually works in the decoder, and why it's necessary for autoregressive training to be efficient.

Key takeaways:
- Encoder-only: bidirectional attention; embeddings + classification
- Decoder-only: causal mask; autoregressive generation; modern LLMs
- Encoder-decoder: cross-attention bridges input and output; translation / summarization
